items.title: Arrival at KIX, transfer to Osaka
items.pace: Evening touchdown — clear immigration and customs, then the JR Haruka straight into Osaka. Nothing else scheduled.
items.tldr: Land at KIX in the evening, ride the Haruka into Osaka, settle in.
items.body:
US passports enter visa-free for tourism (assumed — the intake didn't confirm passport countries). Complete the Visit Japan Web arrival declaration before landing to skip the paper form.

Buy an ICOCA at a KIX ticket machine, then take the JR Haruka limited express to Osaka Station (≈{{fact:haruka-kix-shin-osaka-1800-yen}}, direct). If dinner is wanted on arrival, Kinryu Ramen's Dotonbori Honten runs 24 hours with vending-machine ordering — the low-effort option for a late landing, not a destination meal in its own right.

⚠ The intake gave no landing time, and none of the airport rail links run all night. Once the flight is booked, check the last KIX departures for both the Haruka and the Nankai line against the operators' own timetables, and choose the transfer against the actual landing time rather than the scheduled one — immigration, baggage and the walk to the station all sit between the two. This is the one evening on the trip where a missed connection costs a taxi fare across Osaka Bay.

items.title: Osaka: Castle, Kuromon Ichiba, Dotonbori food crawl
items.pace: Kuromon Ichiba first thing while the aisles are still walkable, the castle late morning into early afternoon, then a three-stop Dotonbori crawl after dark.
items.tldr: A market graze, Osaka Castle by day, then okonomiyaki, kushikatsu and takoyaki after dark.
items.body:
Start at Kuromon Ichiba, two minutes from Namba: before 11am the aisles are still browsable rather than a queue for a 30-minute takoyaki line. Treat it as a grazing first meal, not a sit-down one — the day's real eating is tonight. ⚠ The market's own opening time isn't confirmed in this guide: no primary source for it was reachable within this pass's fetch scope (the market's own site, kuromon.com, is the page to check) and the stalls keep their own hours, so plan this as a mid-morning graze rather than a dawn breakfast.

Then up to Osaka Castle. The keep opens 9:00–18:00 (last entry 17:30), admission {{fact:osaka-castle-admission-1200-yen}} — the surrounding park grounds are free to walk. Arriving late morning off the back of the market avoids both the worst crowds and the midday queue at the ticket counter.

Dinner is a three-stop Dotonbori crawl: Mizuno for okonomiyaki, Kushikatsu Daruma's Dotonbori branch for skewers, and Wanaka for takoyaki to finish. Mizuno takes no reservations and queues nightly, so make it the first stop and budget 30–60 minutes — or put the order the other way round, since Daruma's Dotonbori branch does take weekday bookings between 11:00 and 18:00 for two or more. Kani Doraku's giant mechanical crab sign is worth a photo on the way past, but its ¥5,000–10,000/person course pricing and mixed reviews on ingredient quality make it a landmark to look at, not a meal to book. If the canal-front takoyaki line runs long, Kouga-ryu in nearby Amerikamura is the locals' equivalent at the same price point, minus the wait.

This is also the trip's most rain-proof day — Kuromon and the Dotonbori arcades are roofed and the castle keep is indoors — so if the forecast turns ugly on a Kyoto or Nara day, this is the one to swap toward.

items.title: Kyoto: Fushimi Inari at dawn, Higashiyama, Gion & Pontocho
items.pace: Early start for Fushimi Inari before the tour buses arrive, late morning at Kiyomizu-dera and the Higashiyama slope, a covered lunch at Nishiki, Gion into dusk, then a reserved kaiseki dinner in Pontocho.
items.tldr: Torii gates at sunrise, Kiyomizu-dera's wooden stage by late morning, kaiseki in Pontocho at night.
items.body:
Fushimi Inari Taisha is free and open 24 hours. Arrive by 6:30–7am for the empty version of the famous torii tunnel — by 8am the base is crowded. From the Osaka base that means a first-train morning: JR to Kyoto Station on the Special Rapid, then a few minutes down the JR Nara Line to Inari. ⚠ Check the night before what time the first services actually run — the empty window has closed by 8am, so a missed train costs the whole reason for the early start. Go only as far as the Yotsutsuji junction (~30–45 min up); past it, the summit loop adds another 1.5–2 hours for a view gain most visitors call marginal.

Kiyomizu-dera is open 6:00–18:00 — the temple publishes its hours online but not its fee. ⚠ Admission is widely reported as ¥500 adult / ¥200 elementary–middle school, but no primary or operator source reachable this pass carries that figure, so treat it as indicative and bring cash. Note: this trip does not fall inside a Kiyomizu-dera illumination window — the confirmed 2026 autumn night viewing runs Nov 21–30, after these dates.

Lunch needs planning here: it is roughly eleven hours from the Fushimi Inari start to the Pontocho reservation, and the Higashiyama slope is not where you want to be hunting for a meal. Come down off it and walk west to Nishiki Market: buy from a stall and eat in front of it or inside, which is the market association's own posted request. The arcade is covered end to end, so it is also the one midday hour on this day that a wet forecast can't touch. ⚠ Neither the market association nor any other primary source reachable this pass publishes market-wide hours or closing days — the shops keep their own — so treat the arcade as the plan and any single stall as a preference.

Then back east over Shijo to Gion for the dusk hour — about a fifteen-minute walk, a deliberate backtrack in exchange for a covered meal. The public streets (Hanamikoji, Yasaka Shrine) are open as always; stay off the private alleys around Kosode Koji, posted with a ¥10,000 fine since May 2024.

⚠ Toji's own autumn illumination (Oct 31–Dec 13, 18:00–21:30 with the ticket desk closing at 21:00, ¥1,000) is the one temple illumination that actually falls inside these dates — Kiyomizu-dera's and Eikando's do not. It isn't built into this already-packed day; see the ledger's traveler question on whether to trade something out for it or save it for a future trip.

Dinner: Houshoan in Pontocho. On the October–April menu these dates get, that's the ¥10,000 wagyu-sukiyaki course or the ¥9,500 lavastone yakiniku — the ¥13,000 riverside course a lot of English write-ups quote is a May–September item and won't be on offer. Reserve through its own site or by phone (075-255-2635) — the booking window, cancellation policy and foreign-card acceptance aren't stated on the page, so a follow-up call is worth it. ⚠ Confirm the reservation went through before the day of.

plan_b.body: Heavy rain: drop the Fushimi Inari dawn start — the hillside path is what suffers most — and the Kiyomizu-dera slope with it, and give the whole morning to Nishiki Market's covered arcade (Nishiki-koji St, central Kyoto) instead of the midday hour it already has; Gion and the Pontocho reservation stay as planned. In lighter rain, Nanzenji's Suirokaku aqueduct sits in the same Higashiyama corridor (its November hours and admission are on the Sights card) and two independent firsthand accounts describe it as still worth the walk in a drizzle, just quieter than usual.

items.title: Nara day trip
items.pace: Full day trip to Nara — Todai-ji's Great Buddha Hall, the park's deer, Kasuga Taisha, and a kakinoha-zushi lunch — back to base by evening.
items.tldr: The 15-meter bronze Buddha at Todai-ji, deer in the park, and persimmon-leaf sushi for lunch.
items.body:
The base is Osaka, so the direct run is the Kintetsu Nara Line Limited Express out of Osaka-Namba — {{fact:kintetsu-nara-ltd-express-1200-yen}} (~35–40 min), or the non-limited-express Rapid/Express service on the ¥680 base fare, a little slower with no reservation. (Starting from Kyoto instead, the JR Nara Line rapid runs {{fact:jr-nara-line-kyoto-nara-720-yen}} one-way, ~45 min.)

Todai-ji's Daibutsuden is open 8:00–17:00 in November, admission {{fact:todaiji-admission-800-yen}}. Nara Park deer will bite or headbutt if teased or denied food they can see — only feed them the official shika-senbei sold on-site, and show empty palms when you're out. For a quieter deer encounter than the crowded Nandaimon approach, two independent firsthand accounts point to Asajigahara-en, just north of Ukimido pond.

Kasuga Taisha's main sanctuary is free to visit, 7:00am–5:00pm in November; the inner special-worship area is {{fact:kasuga-taisha-inner-700-yen}}. Lunch: Kakinohazushi Tanaka, a two-minute walk from Kintetsu Nara Station, for kakinoha-zushi (persimmon-leaf-wrapped sushi, a Nara specialty) — no reservation needed.

Both return routes run every 15–30 minutes into the evening; this is not a tight last-train day.
constraints: Kasuga Taisha main sanctuary Nov–Feb hours: 7:00–17:00

plan_b.body: Nara is the trip's one all-outdoor day and there is no full indoor substitute for it — the honest move is to shrink the day, not swap it. Todai-ji's Daibutsuden is the real shelter here: the Great Buddha Hall is an enclosed building, open 8:00–17:00 in November, and it rewards a slow hour rather than a photo stop. Kakinohazushi Tanaka has an in-store tea room, so lunch can be a sit-down rather than a takeaway eaten standing in the wet. In sustained rain, cut Kasuga Taisha's approach and the Asajigahara-en deer detour — both are exposed walks — and head back to base early; return trains run every 15–30 minutes, so leaving costs nothing. ⚠ No weatherproof Nara indoor alternative was verified for this guide: the Nara National Museum's own page returned HTTP 403 on repeated attempts, so its hours and admission are unconfirmed and it isn't recommended blind.

items.title: Arashiyama, then departure prep
items.pace: An early bamboo grove walk and Tenryu-ji's garden, then wind down toward departure — pace this against the actual outbound flight time, which wasn't given at intake, and against the fact that the bags are in Osaka and the morning is in Kyoto.
items.tldr: Arashiyama's bamboo grove before the crowds, then a slow final morning.
items.body:
The Arashiyama Bamboo Grove is a free public path, best before 8am when it's still empty — by 9:30 it's a shuffle. Pair it with Tenryu-ji next door: garden-only admission {{fact:tenryuji-garden-500-yen}} (+¥300 for building access), 8:30am–5:00pm with last admission 4:50pm — and from {{fact:tenryuji-autumn-early-opening-nov-14-30}} the temple opens the Sogenchi garden half an hour early, at 7:30am, for the autumn colour. These dates qualify, so the grove and the garden both fit before the crowds.

Nishiki Market only earns a second visit if Sunday's stop got cut short — it is already in the plan on Nov 15, and a repeat costs this morning's slack. If you do go back: buy from a stall and eat in front of it or inside, rather than walking and eating — the market association's own posted request.

⚠ No outbound flight time was given at intake — and the bags are at the Osaka base while this morning is in Kyoto. Two ways that works: check out with the bags and carry them for the morning, or ride the return leg back through Osaka, since the Haruka is a direct Kansai-Airport service calling at Kyoto, Shin-Osaka, Osaka and Tennoji. Decide which before breakfast, not at 2pm. Either way, Arashiyama sits on the far north-west edge of Kyoto, so a local JR ride back to Kyoto Station comes before the airport leg even starts. Confirm the departure time and work backward from there; this day is written loose on purpose.

plan_b.body: The bamboo grove is the one stop here that rain genuinely spoils — a narrow path with no cover, slick underfoot and shoulder-to-shoulder with umbrellas. Buy Tenryu-ji's building ticket (+¥300 on top of the garden admission) and take the Sogenchi garden from the veranda instead of walking it, then put Nishiki Market back into the morning: it repeats Sunday, but the arcade is covered end to end and is the best rain hour on this side of the trip. If it's a wash-out, this is the right day to cut short — it's the departure day and the schedule is deliberately loose.

title: Health & pharmacy
body:
Police: 110. Fire/ambulance: 119. The Japan Visitor Hotline (050-3816-2787, or +81-50-3816-2787 from abroad) gives multilingual help for medical emergencies, lost property, and other urgent problems around the clock.

Pharmacies (drugstores/薬局) are common in every neighborhood on this itinerary; look for a green cross sign. Convenience stores (7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart) stock basic over-the-counter medicine but not prescriptions.

Nara Park deer will bite, headbutt or kick if teased, cornered, or denied food they can see — only feed the official shika-senbei crackers sold on-site, and raise both empty palms to signal you have none left. Bucks are more assertive during rutting season, which runs through November — exactly this trip's dates.

title: Etiquette & language
body:
Gion's private alleys (around Kosode Koji, on the west side of Hanamikoji) have been off-limits to tourists since May 2024, with a ¥10,000 fine posted for entering or photographing on them — a response to tourists chasing and touching geiko/maiko. The main public streets, Hanamikoji itself and Yasaka Shrine, stay open as normal.

Nishiki Market's own trade association asks visitors not to eat while walking through the arcade — buy, then eat in front of or inside the shop you bought from, not on the move. It's a posted request, not a fined law, but it's worth following in a market that's already crowded.

A slight bow works for most everyday interactions (thanking a shopkeeper, apologizing for a bump); a spoken "sumimasen" (excuse me / sorry) covers getting someone's attention. Remove shoes wherever a raised floor or tatami room signals it, kaiseki restaurants included.
